utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Would you like to call another witness? We are in open session. (Open session Now it is Miss Hollis, very good. Would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Osman Selak. MR. OSMAN SELAK, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, would you take that oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Selak Osman.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th May 1935.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Visegrad, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where is Visegrad located in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnic group or nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Islamic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Director of a business unit of Sokolac, a company in Tuzla with headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your prior occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1955 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your area of specialisation within the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Logistics.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your rank when you left the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, I would like to ask you some questions about your military training and background. You received your initial military schooling at Vojno Tehnicka Academy in Zagreb, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While there you studied technical maintenance of equipment, primarily combat vehicles and tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You graduated from there in 1958 with the rank of 2nd Lieutenant and after that you were assigned to the geographic area of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A 2nd Lieutenant and assigned to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you remain assigned to the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout my service.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where is Banja Luka in relation to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 50 kilometres to the east.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In relation to the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 40 to 42 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were first assigned to Banja Luka, you first held the position of Commander of a Technical Maintenance platoon there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is that a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that you became Commander of the supply platoon of the technical company there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then you became Commander of the logistics platoon at the training area in the Manjaca polygon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Which type of training was conducted there, at the training area in the Manjaca polygon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The training was driving of tanks, firing training, training of infantry units.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "firing training", you are referring to the firing of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Combat vehicles, tanks, APCs and ground artillery.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How close was that training area to what was later to become the Manjaca detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Manjaca camp was in the centre of the training grounds.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the military actually prepare this camp for use as a detention centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not before.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did they do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did it in 1992, towards the end of May and in early June.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was the military who prepared this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was on the training grounds when the inmates did it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the direction of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the commander, superiors. Military police was there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you a photograph, and for the Defence's information this is document 5/14. I would like to have this marked as Prosecution 160 for identification. I would ask that that photograph be called up on to the computer monitor. Colonel Selak, do you recognise the buildings and the location of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are the buildings in the Manjaca training grounds. This is the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the sign that appears in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sign is, it says over the gate "the camp" and the transprohibited in Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 160 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): Colonel Selak, after commanding the logistics platoon at the training centre you were transferred to the Zaluzani barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was a JNA garrison located about eight to 10 kilometres away from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: North of Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of facility was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the centre for the training of drivers for combat vehicles for the entire Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: From 1964 until late 1965, you were the Commander of the maintenance platoon there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At that point you were transferred to the school centre for armoured and mechanized units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was that school located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Banja Luka, in the barracks Bane Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of school was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Military Academy for armoured and mechanized units, a second military school for reserves officers, a school where courses were organised for the Commanders of armoured and mechanized units of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What duties did you perform there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, as part of my, the commander responsible for the regulations on the use of tanks.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What other duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was Deputy Commander of the technical maintenance service in the management of the secondary school centre for armoured and mechanized units.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then in 1977 you became the Deputy Manager of the 993rd Technical Base at Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In August of 1981 you became the Manager of 993rd Technical Base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the Rear Technical Bases were set on 28th December 1989.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your next position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander of 993 Rear Technical Base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until I retired on 10th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the last .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you said that your military speciality was logistics; could you give the court a very brief description of the logistics function in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. The logistics security of the Yugoslav People's Army was based on the materiel reserves of the Yugoslav People's Army and the resources, economic resources, of the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of materiel did you provide to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armaments, ammunition, fuel, supplies, equipment, personal equipment, joint equipment, medicines, services such as maintenance -- all that comes under the logistics support of an army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that in 1989 there was a reorganisation and rear bases were formed such as Rear Base 993. How many such bases were formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, there were 16 such bases.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the other logistics bases in addition to your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with bases in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the command of the first Military District in Belgrade. I did not know others.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Each rear base had a geographic area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within these geographic areas of responsibility, each base provided logistics support to JNA units located within those areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to have this document marked as Prosecution Exhibit 161 for identification, and for the Defence this is map 1. (Document handed). (To the witness): Colonel Selak, would you please look at that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Does that document depict your logistics area of operation before 18th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection? Exhibit 161 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could put that on the elmo, please? Sir, looking at this document, would you please tell us what this area within the dotted line, the area that includes Kozara Mountain, Prijedor, Banja Luka, what does that area represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area indicates the peace time area of responsibility and the logistic support of the units of the corps of the army for which my base provided support in this area.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the wider area that is totally encompassed by this solid red line, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area represents the area of responsibility of the logistics support of the units at the outset of the war and during the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Looking at the area that is marked in solid red, is that an area that was supplied by you logistically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Looking at this exhibit, I note that there are some towns that are located outside of Bosnia, towns in Croatia; these are units that you supplied in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These would be JNA units that you supplied there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These units that you supplied there would be units that were involved in the fighting in Croatia, fighting against Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, within your area of operations or area of responsibility, was the 5th corps also known as the Banja Luka corps within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was that corps headquartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could retrieve the exhibit from the witness? Colonel Selak, I would like to speak with you for a moment about JNA uniforms. During your service in the JNA, what was the regular JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grey, olive green with insignia on shoulders. On their lapels of the uniform there were metal insignia of the branch, of the army. On the caps there was an emblem with a five pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, this uniform that you have just mentioned, are you talking about what is sometimes referred as to as the SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This uniform was solid in colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that there were insignia on the shoulders, I believe? What insignia was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were ranks, insignia for ranks, for superiors.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who would wear the insignia on their shoulders, what categories of personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Insignia was worn there from soldiers, warrant officers, sergeants, staff sergeants and active duty officers from the sergeant to general.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you are talking basically about non-commissioned officers and officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The hat that you mentioned, would this be the same colour as the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1986 or 1987 was a new uniform introduced into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was this uniform called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That uniform was a camouflage uniform, lighter green, dark green. We called them camouflage uniforms. They could not be used in peace time; only under wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to have this document marked as Prosecution Exhibit 162 for identification. This is document 5.1.10. (Document handed). I would ask that that be provided to the witness. If we could call that up on the computer, please, to be shown on the computer monitor? (To the witness): Colonel Selak, Prosecution Exhibit 162 for identification, is that the uniform that you just described to us as the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 162.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 162 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): Colonel Selak, the uniform appears at least in the photograph to have an insignia on the left pocket. Do you see that insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is that insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the insignia of rank which was worn on the left pocket of the camouflage uniform. It is in metal, indicated in metal.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any other insignia authorised for wear on this camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know the man in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Retired Lieutenant Colonel Popovic Bozo, reactivated and Commander of the Manjaca prisoners camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say he was retired Lieutenant Colonel; to your knowledge, had he been in active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an active duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is from Bosnia but by origin a Montenegrin. I am not sure. I think he is from Bosnia, but his parents from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When would he have performed duties as the Commander of the Manjaca detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after the camp was formed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This occurred when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, somewhere at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of July or of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the introduction of this camouflage uniform, was it authorised to wear either uniform daily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except the camouflage uniform, we had olive grey uniform for soldiers that we used during exercises and training, and for units that did not have the necessary number of new camouflage uniforms could use the old ones.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So prior to the outbreak of conflict this uniform was worn for training purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then after the outbreak of conflict, first in Croatia and then in Bosnia, when was it authorised to wear this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after mobilization, it was compulsory to wear this uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Which mobilization are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several and for various units at various times. The first mobilization in my area of responsibility, a part of the educational centre, this was in May '91.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So after that it was authorised to wear this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only for that unit.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The units that were mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have difficulty supplying all of the mobilized units with this camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The smaller units, we had no problems, but later when the whole corps was mobilized we could not immediately provide camouflage uniforms for all the enlisted men. It needed time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you mentioned, the ones you could not supply with camouflage uniforms were allowed to wear the SMB uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What hat would be worn with this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We called it "titovka" and at the top of the cap in peace time we used a five cornered star with the emblem, and later it was a linen insignia, a linen mark, on which was written "JNA".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of insignia was it? Was it just the lettering "JNA" or was there something else on this insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, there was the flag blue, white, red, and across it embroidered the letters "JNA".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For what period of time did "JNA" appear on these caps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very short time. I cannot give you the exact date. I already had problems because of this. I do not know the exact date. I think it was somewhere until end of May '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned this three colour flag; this was the flag of what Republic or entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the flag of the Republic of Serbia or, rather, of the Serb entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to 1991 who besides the JNA was authorised to wear JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence. They were entitled to wear them if they had them and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The military police uniforms in the JNA, did they differ from the regular uniforms in any respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were the same, but the military police wore white belts.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the JNA at any time have any blue camouflage type uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the land forces, no.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What forces had blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, perhaps a part of the Air Force. I did not have such uniforms, nor did I issue them. I do not know who has blue camouflage uniforms. It is outside the standard of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the supposed JNA withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that when the insignia on the hat was changed from the five point star to this flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The five pointed star was eliminated and the letters "JNA" were removed. Later, on the shoulders, the Army of the Republic of Serbia, their insignia were put on the left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was round in shape with the letters "VRS" on it, Army of the Republika Srspka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have mentioned that you did have some difficulty getting enough uniforms to supply everyone. Did this lead to some uniforms that were slightly different in colour from the uniform we see before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to a shortage of camouflage uniforms, production started in various companies of a similar uniform, not using this material but with the same insignia for ranks. These were manufactured by certain factories on the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You, the JNA, issued these uniforms to authorised personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I issued uniforms to the corps and their brigades, and I had no influence on the actual distribution of uniforms at the lower level, so I do not know whom they gave it to, but there was a diversity of uniforms. One could see people wearing uniforms of different colours.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to ask you some questions relating to the organisation of the JNA. In the Yugoslav military or defence structure, the JNA was the primary defence component and it was controlled by the federative authorities of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the JNA was divided into an active duty component and a reserve component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the active duty component contained what categories of personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers doing their regular military service which lasted one year to 15 months, and this underwent a change in the last 10 or 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the active duty component also include civilians who worked for the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were civilians working for the JNA who did not wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The reserve component would have consisted of what categories of personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reserve officers, reserve non-commissioned officers and military conscripts, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within the reserve component, reserve officers would train and perform duties every year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Reserve soldiers would train only cyclically, that is, every so many years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after four years, sometimes earlier on if the need arose for a certain skill, for additional training in new types of weaponry and equipment, but this applied to a smaller number of people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, during your JNA career, you were an active duty officer, not a reserve officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us within the JNA what the NCO ranks were -- the non-commissioned officer ranks, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking of ranks?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers ranks were leader, a corporal and sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I am asking about the non-commissioned officer ranks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the non-commissioned officers, we had a sergeant, sergeant first class, a senior sergeant, staff sergeant, warrant officer and first class warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about the ethnic composition of the Yugoslav People's Army. Within the military, how would you know what ethnic group a military member belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For active duty military, the files -- each member had his own file which was kept in the Brigade or in the corps and in the army command or the military zone. The Commander of the unit had insight at any given time into that file which contained, in addition to personal data, data on national composition which would show where the person came from, where he was born and what ethnic group he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to 1991, to your knowledge, what was the ethnic composition of the officer corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This data was never officially published, but I can say for my unit and make a rough estimate regarding the situation in the Banja Luka corps in which I served. In my base about 90 per cent of the officers were of Serb nationality. The situation was similar at the level of the Banja Luka corps.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As of 1991 and 1992, what change, if any, occurred in that ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the first mobilization was carried out in '91, the ethnic composition reflected the situation on the ground. However, at the end of '91 and in '92 this was seriously disrupted and the ethnic composition of both Commanders and soldiers was 99 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why this increase in the percentage of Serbs in the military as of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war in Croatia, the Croats were first to withdraw from units and they were followed by the Muslims or the Bosniaks, so that there was an ethnically completely clean composition, only individuals remained in their units -- I mean, individual Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These vacancies were then filled by persons of the Serb ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, within this Serb ethnic group, was there any way to determine which of these Serb officers were from Serbia or Montenegro as opposed to being from Bosnia, Croatia or Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could be established in two ways. I am talking about Banja Luka and the Banja Luka region. First, the dialect differs in Serbia from what is spoken in Bosnia, so that you could recognise a Serb, a Montenegrin from Serbia if he was serving in Bosnia. Also, you could recognise Macedonian by his language because it is a different dialect. Also, we knew each other, at least I am talking about us in Banja Luka where I served; and in my superior command in Belgrade, later in Sarajevo, I knew most of the officers because we communicated amongst ourselves for many years, and also I had files from which I could see. I could look at somebody's personal file and see where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was any such breakdown ever made or published for the members of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had any such information.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you were talking about the ethnic composition, you spoke of the active duty force. Do you have any information as to what the ethnic composition was of the reserve officer corps before 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reserve corps in ethnic terms corresponded to the territory of each unit, that is where the recruits came from, so that, for instance, in Banja Luka the ratio among Serbs Croats and Muslims was about 40-20, 25 per cent in favour of the Serbs. The reserve force reflected the composition of the population locally, and this applied to all other localities because by their organisations units are replenished from the territory where they are based.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did this ethnic composition change in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did it change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In such a way that the Muslims and Croats left themselves, but also they were forced out because there were threats of liquidation, as was the case with one of my commanders.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what commander was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander of Ammunition Depot when in March '92 he was threatened, his life was threatened. I urgently replaced him and he demobilized of his own will and he had to flee Banja Luka. Mujajic Alisa is his name, Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And his religious group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Islamic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now the non-Commissioned Officer Corps after 1991 and after, what was its ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are missing the translation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat that please, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my case too there are interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We did not hear any of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, may I repeat my question and ask you then to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The non-Commissioned Officer Corps in 1991 and after, what was the composition of that corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the Non-Commissioned Officer Corps in '91 was replenished from secondary military schools, and they spent longer periods in the places of residence where they were born. The ethnic composition was also majority Serb. Perhaps more than 90 per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to ask you some questions about the ethnic orientation of the JNA. Prior to 1991 were you aware of any indications of discrimination against non-Serbs in such things as selection for important military schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of discriminations were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People complained to me of Bosniak and Croatian ethnic groups, that their children cannot pass the competitions for military schools, especially for secondary military schools and also for the academy because at medical examinations the criteria applied were different. This was not officially stated anywhere, but people complained whose children went for these examinations and I know of several cases, concrete cases.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge was there any type of discrimination in the selection for military schools, advanced military schools for officers who were already in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certain criticisms, especially for the training of officers upon the completion of academy and after the joining the command staff and wartime schools without which no promotion in their career could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What groups were discriminated against in attendance to these schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniaks, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "Bosniaks" to what group are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your own situation looking at 1991 and 1992, were there any changes in the way you were treated during that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What changes were there in your treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During official tours of units and in municipal assemblies where I had to have contact with the authorities in '91, I was always escorted with the assistant for morality, Major Jordan and later Lieutenant Colonel, and the Chief of Staff of Security Captain First Class Fricer Ivan. The official position was that they were going to protect me. However, I established that in fact they were there to control my behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you said Major Jordan was one of the escorts. What was his ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Pavlovic Jordan. Later he was Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Major Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his status? What he an active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He belonged to the active duty corps.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, from Uzice in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned someone else who supported you, a captain First Class Fricer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fricer Ivan, Chief of Staff of Security in the command of my base.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he an active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active duty.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Slovac, born from the surroundings of Pakrac in Croatia and he is still an active duty officer in the army of the Republika Srspka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now at the time that you were being escorted by these officers, did you feel, yourself feel any personal threat to your safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I had no reason for that, at least that was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any specific locations in 1991 or 1992 from which you were prevented from going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when the genocide was carried out in Kozarac near Banja Luka on May 27th 1992 I was supposed to go to the fuel depot near Prijedor in Brezicani. My Chief of Staff, Colonel Cendic, told me that I should not go there because I could be liquidated because the population in Kozarac had been massacred and my presence might be misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who told you this, your Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff Colonel Cendic Radislav, Rade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Cendic, what his status? Was he active duty or reserve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, from Cacak Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He told you this on what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were given approval to use federal reserves of fuel at the Brezicani near Prijedor. I was supposed to go with the chief of the technical service to organise the takeover of part of the fuel that was given to us, and when my Chief of Staff heard of this Colonel Cendic and because to reach Brezicani you have to go via Kozarac, he told me that I should not go there. He did not prohibit me from going but he said that I should not go there for reasons of personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was end of May or beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now in addition to these escorts that you had, were there any other differences and treatment towards you in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that there were regular meetings in the corps command. On the Corps Commander premises it was Lieutenant General Nikola Uzelac. Those meetings were attended by his assistants and myself as the commander of the logistics base. Until September '91 I was regularly invited to the briefings which began at 7 o'clock in the morning. However, later on I was invited to attend at 7.30. By that time they would have already finished discussing some questions and after I would arrive they would discuss the logistics with me. I realised that as a mistrust towards me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that this was when General Uzelac was Corps Commander. Are you talking about the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was an active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was from Croatia, from some place.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These other officers who continued to attend the meeting at 7 o'clock in the morning, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were assistants of the commander. I know their names. I can list them. They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there some incident that occurred just prior to your being called in to these meetings a half hour late?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those meetings continued to begin at 7 and I was invited at half past 7. What they discussed during that half hour I can only guess. I saw no written document about that, so I do not know what questions they discussed then, but I can assume what it could be about.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said this began around September or October of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there some incident that had occurred just prior to this involving General Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a case when General Uzelac requested me to issue weapons to TO units in Sipovo and Mrkonjic. Those units were not mobilized and under the then regulations they were not entitled to those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you issue the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when official orders came from the superior command the armaments were issued to Sipovo, Mrkonjic and Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sipovo, the TO units there were comprised of what ethnic group or groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the municipality of Sipovo was I think about 65 per cent Serbs and the rest were Muslims and Croats. In Mrkonjic Grad it was similar.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Jajce 34, 35 per cent were Muslims, about 34 per cent were Croats and some 20 per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was the composition of the TO unit at the time these weapons were provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident involving General Uzelac and General Arsic which concerned the situation in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the situation in Bihac. It was 15th November '91,, but it was not General Arsic but General Adzic. So it was the Chief of Staff. It is him you mean?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I misspoke. I meant General Adzic. Were you present at a meeting where this situation was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a meeting in the army club in Banja Luka attended by General Adzic, General Raseta from Zagreb. Then representatives of the Knin Corps, of the Army Republic Serb Krajina and some assistants to the Banja Luka Corps Commander. I was also present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At that meeting did General Adzic give you and General Uzelac a task concerning Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the meeting General Adzic ordered General Uzelac and myself to go to Bihac to quiet down the political situation in Bihac, organise a meeting with representatives of municipalities in the region of Bihac and representatives of political parties in the region of Bihac, saying, "You, Nikola", that is Uzelac's name, "You, Nikola, take care of the Serbs and Osman will take care of the Turks."

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you reply to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I responded spontaneously and said: "I guess you mean the Muslims, Command General?" Nobody had any comment, neither he had any. The same thing was repeated on the same day at the airport, Mahovljani at Banja Luka when General Uzelac and I were seeing General Adzic off to Belgrade. He repeated that saying that Nikola would take care of the Serbs and Osman of the Turks. I reacted again and said: "You mean Muslims?" and he did not say anything, but General Uzelac only looked at me with hatred and that was when problems began and when mistrust towards me began.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, General Adzic, you said he was on the General Staff. Was that the General Staff located in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Uzelac was the Commander of the 5th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army in Banja Luka, and the army command was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, and General Adzic, was he on the General Staff located in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Adzic was the Chief of the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he an active duty officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active duty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he is from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cacko, Herzegovina Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to move to another line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. I appreciate that. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 a.m. (The court adjourned until the following day). 20 23 24 25
